en: Volume Three, Part One.
Composed by Li Tongxuan of the Great Tang at the Northern Capital.
The Stage of the Ten Practices. The Stage of the Ten Practices.
First is the Practice of Joy.
To the south there is a land called Trimukha; therein dwells a bhikṣu named Sudarśana.
The meaning of "south" is as explained previously.

The land is named "Three Eyes" because it clarifies the Dharma-eye, the Wisdom-eye, and the Insight-eye; since this spiritual friend, within this practice, constantly benefits sentient beings by means of these three eyes, it is therefore called "Three Eyes."
"Eye" refers to the eye.
With the clarity and purity of the Dharma-eye, one constantly perceives the Dharmakāya;
with the wisdom-eye, one knows the faculties, skillfully discerning the capacities of sentient beings.
The wisdom-eye discerns and clearly perceives what is correct and what is deviant.
By means of these three eyes, one acts without delusion;

yet if one lacks these three eyes, one remains perpetually confused and nothing one does will be free from defilement. How could such a person be capable of benefiting others by leading them away from the entanglements of the afflictions?
That land is distinguished by the gate of the virtuous conduct of spiritual friends and is named "The Three Eyes.

There is a bhikṣu named Sudarśana; because he knows the faculties [of beings] with these three eyes and bestows benefit according to those faculties without teaching haphazardly, he is named Sudarśana.
Why is it that at the beginning of these ten practices, the bhikṣu is placed first?

Because he practices the vidyāsthāna (fields of knowledge), having first attained clarity through the three eyes, and being free from defilement regarding the objects of mind within the world, he is called a bhikṣu.
Because the bhikṣu is free from defilement, this is the meaning of liberation.
At the beginning of these ten practices, the mention of the "bhikṣu" signifies the principle of non-attachment in one's conduct within this realm.

At the beginning of the Ten Abodes, the Bhikṣu Virtuous Cloud atop Mount Wonderful Peak represents the emergence from meditative concentration into contemplation, signifying the transcendence of the mundane through the exhaustion of the signs of light.

In the first of the ten dedications, there was a merchant who sold incense named Blue Lotus (*Utpala*). Because he clearly demonstrated how those whose minds are largely entangled in worldly existence may enter the cycle of birth and death to accomplish the practice of great compassion—dwelling in the world while knowing the truth and remaining undefiled—he was called Blue Lotus.
To express this in conventional terms, it is like the case of Vimalakīrti and others.

At the beginning of the Ten Grounds (Daśabhūmi), there is the Night Goddess Vasanti, which here is translated as "Mistress of Spring's Birth. This illustrates the practice of great compassion on the Ten Grounds: she constantly dwells within the long night of birth and death, presiding over all sentient beings and causing the sprouts of goodness to grow.
Furthermore, he is the presiding deity who causes the sprouts of crops to grow in the spring.

When Sudhana arrived at the country of Tryakṣa, he searched everywhere throughout its cities, towns, villages, hamlets, marketplaces, rivers, sources, mountains, and valleys; among these, "cities" can be understood as follows.

Regarding "neighborhoods" (*lín*), the *Shangshu Dazhuan* states: "Five households constitute a neighborhood (*lín*); three neighborhoods constitute a group (*péng*); three groups constitute a village (*lǐ*); and five villages constitute a town (*yì*)."
"This is the system established by the Yu and Xia dynasties.
The rest may be understood accordingly.
Thus did Sudhana seek and investigate, clearly observing that all phenomena—whether tranquil or turbulent—are without intrinsic substance, remaining unattached in all places.
When a bhikṣu walks back and forth in meditation within the forest, it signifies that the myriad practices are as bright as a forest providing shade, thereby adorning all existence.
Just as the earth possesses forests to adorn the true realm, so too does a person possess practice to adorn their own self and benefit others.
One who traverses the path of coming and going clearly realizes that the essence of reality abides neither in birth-and-death nor in the liberation of nirvana.

Therefore, those bhikṣus in the prime of their youth, by means of this clarity, remain undisturbed by worldly praise or blame and exhaustlessly benefit sentient beings; thus they possess the vigor of youth, beauty, and an upright appearance that is pleasing to behold.

His hair is deep blue-black, curling to the right without disorder; his crown is marked by a fleshy protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*); his skin is golden in color; his neck bears three lines; his forehead is broad and even; and his eyes are long and wide like blue lotuses. Thus, he is fully endowed with these thirty-two marks. Internally adorned with the eye of Dharma, the eye of knowledge, and the eye of wisdom, he manifests virtuous conduct externally. With compassion, gentleness, and joy, he knows the faculties of beings to guide their rebirth. Having attained these marks as a result of retribution, his body is thus adorned with the thirty-two marks—the true fruit of karmic fruition.

When he was walking in formal meditation (caṅkrama), neither too slowly nor too quickly, walking with deliberate composure, he was surrounded before and behind by a multitude of ten classes of beings—immeasurable devas, nāgas, the eight assemblies, Śakra, Brahmā, and the world-protectors—who had been summoned and converted by his practice.

Regarding the presiding deities of the directions who revolve according to the quarters: the eight directions—Zhen, Xun, Li, Kun, Dui, Qian, Kan, and Gen—along with the two directions of above and below, constitute the ten directions; in each of these, there is a deity who follows and revolves along with them as they move.

Furthermore, within the symbolic representation of phenomena (*dharmas*), *Zhen* (the trigram for thunder) represents wood. This is because wood inherently contains the principles of the ten directions; thus, by taking ten and subtracting eight, one obtains the character for "wood" (*mu*).

*Zhen* signifies sound, vibration, the Azure Dragon, auspiciousness, springtime growth, illumination, and the foremost of all virtues; therefore, these dharmas take the east as their primary direction.
The south is associated with detachment (*li*); it is emptiness, it is correctness, it is the sun, it is the eye, it is the mind, it is literary composition, and it is brilliant clarity.
If one realizes that the mind is empty and void, then there will be wisdom, literary brilliance, and clarity.
Therefore, the phrase "asking one and knowing ten" signifies the flourishing and clarity of wisdom.
By using this "tortoise with ten companions" to ask one and know ten, it symbolizes the brilliance of wisdom.
The North corresponds to the trigram Kan, to water, to the Black Warrior (Xuánwǔ), and to the initial emergence of light.

This direction is designated by the character "North" (běi) because it marks the first differentiation between light and darkness; thus, in the eleventh month, the first yang-line arises. This represents the beginning of the initial division between light and darkness, wherein darkness departs and light arrives, as light and darkness turn away from one another.

Furthermore, it signifies being situated precisely in the position of Xuánwǔ (the North), a time of delusion, folly, and treachery; a state where good and evil are not in harmony, where there is neither trust nor compliance, and likewise where light and darkness do not accord—all of which are mutually opposed. Hence, it is called the character "North" (Běi).
On the back of the bhikṣu Sāgaradhvaja, two vehicles emerge to symbolize this.
Furthermore, the trigram Kan represents solidity and water; that water skillfully benefits all things is entirely the meaning of revolving according to the directions.
The paths of good and evil exist throughout the ten directions.
In the northeast, there are mountains, stones, obstructions, young males, and the ignorant.
The beginning of the year and the end of the year are contained therein; the *chou* and *wei* hexagrams oppose one another, serving as the boundary between Yin and Yang.
Metal’s tomb is in *Chou*, and Wood’s tomb is in *Wei*; the Sun is born in *Yin*, and the Moon is born in *Shen*.
Because *gen* (艮) represents the mountain, it symbolizes that the mountain is high and difficult to ascend.
The character for "person" (*ba* 巴) is used to form the character for *gen*.
If this symbolizes the difficulty of ascending the Holy Path, it means that when the mind is pure and immovable like a mountain, the Right Path manifests.
One immediately uses *gen* (艮) to arrest the mind; the manifestation of the Right Path constitutes the meaning of *gen*, all of which carries the sense of turning according to the directions.
The southeast direction is *xun* (巽), representing wind, the eldest daughter, speech, and the teaching of the winds; therefore, *xun* presides over *xin-chou* and *xin-wei*.
The Earthly Branch *Chou* (Ox) represents the young boy, and *Wei* (Sheep) represents the multitude; these signify faith and compliance.
*Ming* (Brightness) and *Xun* (Gentle-Influence) represent speech and the wind of instruction, used to transform the multitude.

When the ignorant young boy has already attained the Way, his virtue accords with Heaven and Earth and he requires no further teaching. Therefore, the mouth emits the wind [of breath] to bestow verbal instruction for the purpose of determining the right from the wrong.
When both "is" and "is not" are exhausted and all verbal expressions have ceased, the two together form the character *xùn* (巽).
This is the general outline.

The dharmas of the ten directions are immeasurable; the dharmas of a single direction fully possess those of the ten directions. Their interpenetrating natures are so complex and varied that they can never be fully articulated. They merely revolve according to worldly and world-transcending dharmas, turning in accordance with specific circumstances.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The presiding deities of the directions follow their respective quarters; this is the principle of revolving.
This clarifies that dharmas have no fixed essence, but adapt and transform according to circumstances.
This clarifies that within this stage, one acts with mastery according to worldly affairs, turning and adapting as appropriate to each situation.
As for "guiding those who come before," it clarifies that one guides all sentient beings by prioritizing the skillful application of teachings and practices.
The foot-walking deity holds a precious lotus flower to support his feet; the deity symbolizes wisdom, for amidst the myriad practices he dwells in the world without defilement.
This clarifies that the essential nature of his practice is stainless.
The forest deity of the Jambū-dhvaja grove rained down clouds of various flowers.
This grove is situated near Lake Anavatapta; it symbolizes how the myriad practices are like a forest, providing shelter and shade for all living beings.
He does not practice a single course, yet he dwells in immeasurable practices to deliver sentient beings.
"Flower" refers to practice.
As for the Spirit of Exhaustless Light, who radiates light to shatter darkness, it is because he constantly uses wisdom to destroy all delusive obscurity.
The earth goddess Akṣayakośa manifests various treasuries of jewels so that all sentient beings may cultivate wholesome karma and open the treasury of wisdom.

The space goddess Samantābhāsagaganālaṃkāra adorns space by using the wisdom of universal radiance to deliver sentient beings; she causes all beings to practice the conduct of emptiness, shatter all delusive darkness, and attain immeasurable merit, thereby achieving self-adornment.
The ocean deity Guṇasāgara showers maṇi jewels because he purifies the defilements of sentient beings through the practice of great compassion.

The Sumeru mountain deity Vimalagarbha prostrates with reverence, bowing his body and joining his palms; manifesting the excellence of his own clear wisdom, he constantly practices humility and respect, free from any sense of self-conceit.
The Wind Deity of Unobstructed Power rains down exquisite fragrant flowers.

This is the deity of the southeast (Śun), who, through clear wisdom, skillfully expounds the teachings of the wind; those who hear it are filled with joy—this is the significance of the fragrant flowers.
Xun represents wind and the teaching of righteousness.
The Night Spirit presiding over the harmony of spring adorns her body by prostrating herself on the ground; this signifies that all virtuous deeds constitute adornment.
"All" means that one's conduct never departs from the ground of fundamental wisdom and is constantly awakened.
The Lord of Day deity, holding a mani-jewel banner that universally illumines all directions, dwells in space.
Regarding the emission of great radiance: the formless Dharma-body is taken as space, and the light of fundamental wisdom is taken as the substance of the mani-jewel banner.

Taking the stainless, pure radiance of the intrinsic nature of wisdom as its illuminating essence, it clarifies all practices as well as the mind and its objects; it constantly employs the fundamental wisdom of universal radiance to shine universally throughout the ten directions, such that not a single dharma can be apprehended, yet it delivers all sentient beings through myriad practices without ever departing from this wisdom.
Always remaining undeluded regarding the mind and its objects, one is thus able to remain unstained by and unattached to the world.
Abiding in the world to teach and transform sentient beings, one constantly practices these ten modes of conduct without fault.
These ten deities represent the practice of the ten *pāramitās* through which divine wisdom engages with the world, so that practitioners may emulate them.
From the words "I have heard the Holy One," and so forth, [the text] requests the Dharma.
The bhikṣu replied:

"As for my saying 'I am young in years and have recently left the household life,' this clarifies that I have just begun from the Ten Abodes and have newly entered the commencement of the Ten Practices."

Throughout this life of mine, while purifying my practice of the Brahma-faring under Buddhas as numerous as the sands of thirty-eight Ganges Rivers, I have taken the three dharmas—the Wisdom Eye, the Dharma Eye, and the Prajna Eye—as thirty distinct practices through their various manifestations; by means of these three dharmas, I am able to eliminate the ten types of ignorance within mind, objects, and consciousness.

Because all mental objects, minds, and consciousnesses observed through these three dharmas do not depart from what is known and seen by the Dharma-eye, the Wisdom-eye, and the Prajna-eye, and because they are constantly in accord with the practice of the Eightfold Noble Path, it is said that he purified his Brahma-conduct under Buddhas as numerous as the sands of thirty-eight Ganges Rivers.

Regarding all afflictions of false views as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, when observed with the three eyes, there is not a single dharma that is not liberated, because nothing is apart from what is known and seen by the Dharma-eye, the Wisdom-eye, and the Insight-eye; nor is there a single dharma that is not pure, because body, speech, and mind are entirely pure. Therefore, it is said that he cultivated the Brahma-faring under Buddhas as numerous as the sands of thirty-eight Ganges Rivers.
By means of the purity of the three eyes, all objects of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are universally purified; this is called the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. The Sūtra says:

"In some instances, at the place of a Buddha, one may purify the Brahma-conduct for a single day and night, or even for seven days and nights, half a month, a month, a year, or even for unspeakable kalpas; one may purify the Brahma-conduct until entering the state of non-attainment, yet one still sees that Buddha attain equal and perfect enlightenment, and each of his various teachings without any confusion. This is because the moon has no beginning or end and possesses neither root nor branch; within the entirety of mind and its objects, not a single dharma is seen as being either right or wrong, subject or object—this is the purification of Brahma-conduct.
"Brahman" means purity.

To thoroughly understand that the nature of the mind and its objects is free from defilement or purity, and neither right nor wrong, and to constantly maintain such contemplation, is to purely cultivate the Brahma-faring (brahmacarya) in the presence of all Buddhas. Because one's own mind and its objects are entirely pure, one is indeed a Buddha.
A practitioner can never achieve Buddhahood by maintaining the notion of "right" regarding themselves and "wrong" regarding others;
even if they exert themselves through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, they will not escape birth and death.
How can both mind and environment be purified?
By employing the three eyes as appropriate, one sustains the world.
A practitioner should constantly observe the world with these three eyes, causing the mind, environment, and consciousness to become the activity of wisdom.
With a mind and heart pure, compassionate, and harmonious, one leads sentient beings without weariness.
Why should one worry about anything?
All Buddha-dharmas will naturally become clear.
"From 'I only know this Bodhisattva’s liberation door of the inexhaustible lamp' onwards, it clarifies the recommendation of his virtues to those who preceded him, further causing them to advance.

By means of the Dharma-eye, the Wisdom-eye, and the Prajna-eye, he constantly illuminates what is present before him, ensuring that the mind and its objects do not become deluded; thus, the seeds of emotional consciousness are entirely extinguished, and only wisdom manifests. This is called the Dharma-door of the Inexhaustible Lamp."

Furthermore, by using a single lamp to ignite hundreds of thousands of lamps, all that was dark becomes bright, and this brightness never comes to an end; therefore, it is called the "Inexhaustible Lamp.
In this stage, the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) is primary, while the other nine perfections serve as its companions.
The second is the practice of benefiting others.
To the south there is a land called Yaśasvinī;
the meaning of "south" is as explained previously.

As for the name of the kingdom being "Renowned" (Yaśasvin): it was because the wisdom and virtue of the youth Vijñānagati were so lofty and far-reaching that there was nothing he did not understand; whether it be writing, mathematics, calculation, technical skills, or various arts—indeed, all worldly methods for benefiting others—he mastered them thoroughly. Because his fame spread afar on this account, the kingdom was named Renowned.

The youth is named "Sovereign" (Īśvara) because, having attained the life of immortality, he cannot be thwarted or destroyed by any worldly phenomena; within the cycle of birth and death, he manifests forms according to the capacities of beings with complete mastery, and is therefore called "Sovereign."
Regarding those on the river islets: a place in the water fit for habitation is called a *zhou* (island) when large, and a *zhu* (islet) when small; a very small islet is called a *zhi*.
As for gathering sand to play, it serves to clarify the methods of calculation, allowing one to count and know the number of grains according to how much sand is gathered.

Within this stage, the dharmas of the Bodhisattva’s mastery of knowledge consist of ten types: first, writing; second, calculation; third, sealing; fourth, medicine; fifth, craftsmanship; sixth, the compounding of elixirs; seventh, agriculture; eighth, commerce; ninth, physiognomy; and tenth, knowing the faculties and capacities of others to instruct them accordingly. Possessing these ten dharmas, he benefits sentient beings.
The number *ayuta* is one trillion in this land;
*nayuta* is one hundred million in this land.
As for the remaining numerical values, they have not yet been translated from the Sanskrit original.
From the passage "I have only known these various crafts and supernormal powers" onwards, this is the stage of advancing by inferring [the Buddha's] virtues.
In this stage, the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) is primary, with the other nine perfections serving as its companions.

In the stage of the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*), one contemplates the ocean of birth and death through the observation of the twelvefold dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) as the ocean of Buddha-wisdom;
this constitutes the essence of the precepts (*śīla-svabhāva*). These ten practices of conduct constitute the essence of the precepts, thereby accomplishing deeds that bring benefit to others.

The third is the stage of Non-Contradictory Practice (*aviruddhacaryā*), which takes the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) as its primary focus, with the other nine perfections as its companions.
The meaning of "South" is as explained previously.
There is a great city named Sāgaravihāra; whereas the previous two stages were referred to as "countries," why is this stage referred to as a "city"? To clarify this: [text continues]

However, that which is known through the wisdom and virtue of the *yogācāra* constitutes the kingdom; now, at this stage, protecting the actions of body, speech, and mind through patience so as not to allow arrogance to arise is called the city.
The city is named Sāgarāvasthita; it signifies that the mind of one who has subdued their pride is like the ocean, which receives all streams without rejecting anything.

The laywoman is named Paripūrṇā; she is so named because she is fully endowed with generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and loving-kindness and compassion—possessing these five dharmas, she is called "Complete."

Regarding the residence in which one dwells within this city: it signifies that through the practice of clear patience (*kṣānti*), one is adorned internally and does not dwell on the external; thus, one is "within the city.

That the residence occupied is adorned on all four sides with immeasurable varieties of precious jewels signifies that by single-mindedly harboring the patience for the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*) within, one invokes and attracts the adornment of immeasurable merit.

As for the upāsikā seated upon the jewel throne: she takes patience as the substance of the throne; her flourishing youth, beautiful countenance, and upright, pleasing appearance are the adornments resulting from the retribution of patience.
Wearing plain clothing with hair hanging down and having no necklaces upon the body signifies the abandonment of external adornments to clarify the state of patience (*kṣānti*).

As for the physical marks, majestic virtue, and radiance, these result from the power of the vehicle evoked by the will and virtue of the practice of patience; therefore, one's appearance is pleasing.

That his dwelling is vast and spacious, with four gates opening from a single room, signifies that he practices patience and bestows benevolence with great magnanimity, and that his four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) and four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa*) are limitless.

A single small vessel was placed before the seat; when the infinite multitudes from all worlds came to eat, each obtained food according to their own faculties and attained the Way, with each receiving a distinct portion.

By means of the patience of the Dharma, giving, precepts, compassion, and humility, one is free from self-aggrandizement and arrogance; thus, rather than being a vessel of small capacity, one’s merit becomes vast and one bestows it boundlessly.
If one can maintain a mind of patience like space, the adornment of its merit will never be exhausted.

Thus the verse says: "Practicing patience, body and mind have neither center nor periphery; removing views, great and small, they are like empty space. Their minds are equanimous, without high or low; even the Dharma-gift of ten particles is inexhaustible."

This section elucidates the gate of patience within the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*). The ten thousand maidens collectively represent the practice of patience, gentleness, and harmonious joy; they are symbolized by women.
The fact that their retinue consists of millions of asaṃkhyeyas illustrates that the practice of patience, compassion, and mildness has become all-pervasive.

From the passage "Since I have only known this Bodhisattva’s liberation door of the inexhaustible treasury of merit" onwards, it clarifies the advancement through the recommendation of virtues; it demonstrates that the single door of patience is itself the fulfillment of all practices and the fulfillment of all treasuries of merit.
The fourth is the practice of being unyielding, for which the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*) is primary and the other nine are its companions.
The meaning of "South" is as explained previously.
There is a city named Great Flourishing (*Mahodaya*), which elucidates the perfection of diligence.
Because he extensively practiced the two kinds of giving—material wealth and the Dharma—his deeds were all-pervasive; thus, the city was named Da-xing (Great Flourishing).

The householder was titled Ming-zhi (Wisdom-Intelligence) because, through his wisdom, he conformed to worldly customs and skillfully practiced the two kinds of giving to benefit all sentient beings; hence, he was named Ming-zhi.

Within the city, at a marketplace on a crossroads, Sudhana sat upon a throne of seven precious jewels atop a seven-jeweled platform; that throne was adorned with ten kinds of ornaments, as described extensively in the sutra.
This is because they all arise as the retribution for practicing the ten *pāramitās*.

As for the previous statement that the seven-jeweled terraces serve as the substance of the seats, this clarifies that the myriad practices take the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) as their essential substance.

The seven factors of enlightenment are: first, the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena; second, the factor of enlightenment of energy; third, the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness; fourth, the factor of enlightenment of rapture; fifth, the factor of enlightenment of tranquility; sixth, the factor of enlightenment of concentration; and seventh, the factor of enlightenment of equanimity.
Because fundamental wisdom constitutes the body of the elder, it is called "clear wisdom.
As for the "householder" (gṛhapati), he dwells in the world yet remains unstained by it; therefore, he is named a householder.

By means of this clear wisdom, one dwells in the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*), accomplishes immeasurable gateways of sublime practice, and performs deeds of self-benefit and benefit for others that lead to spiritual advancement.

Illuminating the contemplation of all practices, one remedies habitual tendencies and resolves delusion; with tireless diligence, one achieves great loving-kindness and great compassion—all of which have as their fundamental essence the non-conceptual wisdom (*anabhisaṃskāra-jñāna*) that is the stainless, pure, and white nature of the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā-svabhāva*).

Based on the strength or weakness of the habitual tendencies of affliction and purification, as well as the aspiration for the supramundane mind, one comes to recognize the obstacles that prevent the perfection of the increase or decrease of compassion. Thus, the names of the progressive practices—the ten abodes (*vihāra*), ten conducts (*caryā*), ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), ten stages (*bhūmi*), and the two levels of Equal Enlightenment and Wondrous Enlightenment*—are established as models for practitioners, enabling students to emulate them so that they do not err regarding the teachings. *(Note: "Two levels" refers to *samyak-sambodhi-bhūmi* and *tathāgata-bhūmi*.)*

Therefore, he sat upon a seven-jeweled platform at the crossroads of the marketplace; with the seven factors of enlightenment as the substance of the seat and clarifying the four means of integration and the four immeasurable minds, it was thus named the "Crossroads."
Using the seven factors of enlightenment to encompass the ten pāramitās and immeasurable practices is called "Adorned with Various Jewels.
To constantly dwell within the afflictions of birth and death is to be in the marketplace.
To clarify the practice of diligence in this stage, one should thus engage in the two gates of giving: the giving of material wealth and the giving of the Dharma.
When Sudhana requested the teaching, the householder directed him to observe the infinite variety of the assembled multitude and the differing desires and inclinations of those who had come.

After he had exhorted them to observe this, the householder focused his mind for a moment and looked up into the sky; everything they required descended from the void, and the entire assembly was fully satisfied. This demonstrates that the very essence of wisdom is emptiness, and all karmic fruits and rewards are illusorily produced from that empty wisdom.
By looking up at the void with this, one symbolizes that the ocean of merit and all virtues produced by illusory blessings arise from this wisdom of emptiness;
thus, by contemplating its source, one causes [the practitioner] to know the cause from which the fruits of retribution and merit are born.

Great kindness, great compassion, and the great relinquishment of wealth and Dharma all arise from the wisdom of emptiness; all myriad practices are born from the wisdom of emptiness, and it is the same for all sentient beings and their karmic fruits.

It enables the practitioner to skillfully understand that all meritorious fruits and rewards of the mind and its objects, as well as the causes and effects of the conduct of all sentient beings, all arise from the wisdom of emptiness.

Sentient beings fail to understand this and falsely create ignorance, thereby performing good and evil deeds; they become deluded regarding the wisdom of emptiness and transmigrate through birth and death.

Those who realize this dharma attain great clear wisdom and constantly accord with worldly conventions while practicing compassion. The ocean of all merits—the two kinds of giving, material wealth and the Dharma—becomes vast and inexhaustible, arriving according to thought, for it arises from this wisdom of emptiness.

Therefore, one must observe this so that students may recognize the fundamental source and emulate it; thus, they remain unstained in their practice, just as a lotus flower is worthy of contemplation yet remains unstained by the water in which it dwells.

Within the first ten stages (*bhūmi*), the fourth is the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*). This refers to how the elder Megha, at a marketplace, taught the "Gate of Adornment of the Wheel of Syllables" to an assembly of ten thousand people. He caused them to study various wholesome worldly knowledges, so that they might comprehend worldly designations, writing, syllables, and meanings; how all names arise from one another’s essence, such that each single name contains all names, mutually generating and arising, while their fundamental nature is essentially non-existent.

Now, within the Ten Practices, the fourth is the Practice of Being Unyielding, wherein one practices the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*). Using the wise householder in the marketplace and thoroughfares as an analogy, one employs the four methods of attraction (*saṃgraha-vastu*) to perform the practice of gathering sentient beings through the two kinds of giving—material wealth and the Dharma—which arises from the wisdom of emptiness.
The remaining details are fully explained in the sutra.

From the passage beginning, "Since I have known only this liberation door of the treasury of merit produced with every thought according to one's inclination," it clarifies the advancement through the transfer of merit.
The fifth is the practice of being free from delusion and confusion; the perfection of dhyāna (meditative concentration) is the primary factor, with the other nine as its companions.
The meaning of "south" is as explained previously.

The great city named Siṃhāsana (Lion Throne) clarifies that meditative concentration can give rise to great wisdom; because one preaches the definitive Dharma for destroying birth and death within the cycle of saṃsāra and amidst the great assembly, attaining fearlessness, it is called Siṃhāsana.
This wisdom is clarified as not coming from external dependence on others, but being manifested through the tranquil stabilization of one's own mind;
therefore, it is named the Lion’s Seat (*siṃhāsana*). Wisdom is the lion.

In the marketplace, Sudhana saw the elder Ratnacūḍa, who, to demonstrate that this stage does not abide in the essence of dhyāna, was drawing in and guiding all sentient beings amidst the turmoil of birth and death.

Therefore, the elder took Sudhana by the hand and led him to his residence, showing him the house: it was composed of radiant pure gold, with walls of white silver and a palace of crystal; its multi-storied pavilions were made of deep blue lapis lazuli, its pillars of exquisite *śaṅkhaśilā* gems, and it was adorned throughout with millions of kinds of jewels. A lion throne was made of red pearl *maṇi* gems, with a canopy of *maṇi* and a net of pearls spread over it.
The agate jewel-pools were filled with fragrant water, and immeasurable jewel-trees stood in rows all around.
That residence was vast and spacious, with ten stories and eight gates.

Sudhana observed them in succession; because this was a supporting fruit born as the retribution for the merit of the great wisdom of the dhyāna-body and the practice of the Eightfold Path, he knew the cause by observing the fruit.
When Sudhana contemplates the causes and effects of dwelling in the abode of retribution, he immediately attains the path he has cultivated.

The Master of the Treatise says in verse: “The meditative mind is naturally pure, serving as its own radiance; Its self-nature is stainless, like genuine gold. Vast and penetrating like space, without limit or boundary— This is the abode of the wise.”

With the eye of wisdom, one universally contemplates all phenomena: they are pure and stainless, without center or periphery; in all phenomena, neither grasping nor rejecting can be found—this is the boundary wall of the wise.

Realizing that the nature of the realm of form-objects is non-existent, the mind-king is skillfully cultivated and named the Palace; pure wisdom clearly perceives and illuminates the world, universally shining upon all phenomena as a Pavilion.

Constantly amidst all that is seen and heard, always without grasping or rejecting, and without wavering; though able to see all forms and hear all sounds, not hearing within hearing is the precious pillar.

The intrinsic nature of the objective realm of form is fundamentally without self-nature; the wise take this as the substance of their seat, whereby they may sit within the gates of worldly toil throughout the ten directions, becoming great wisdom untainted by defilement.
Having perfected great wisdom and fearlessness, this is the wise one’s lion throne.
Skillfully setting up the net of teaching to filter out sentient beings, his mind is ever pure, filled with fragrant water.
The palace has ten stories and eight gates; the Ten Perfections and Eightfold Rightness are its conduct.

In the lowest story, food and drink are provided; in the second, the gift of precepts serves as precious robes; in the third, the jewels of patience are flower garlands; in the fourth, kindness, compassion, vigor, and wisdom are the women; in the fifth, dhyāna and prajñā constitute exquisite adornment, where Bodhisattvas of the Five Stages who have attained universal illumination dwell; in the sixth, pure wisdom is the wondrous vehicle of emptiness, where Bodhisattvas of the Sixth Stage reside.

The seventh stage is the realm of expedient means within birth and death; the eighth stage is the sovereign mastery of effortless wisdom; the ninth stage is the abode of the Dharma King for one more lifetime; and the tenth stage is the complete fulfillment of the fruit of Buddhahood.

Training in this sequence, there is ultimately no beginning, middle, or end; by means of this gateway of samādhi, wisdom, and dhāraṇī, one abides in the mastery of knowledge, which is neither empty nor existent.
Sudhana said, "What roots of goodness did you plant to obtain such a karmic reward?
The elder replied:

“Good son! I recall that in the past, beyond as many eons as there are atoms in a buddha-field, there was a world named Perfectly Adorned. There, a Buddha appeared, titled Boundless Radiance King of Universal Adornment of the Dharma Realm, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, whose ten epithets were complete.”
"When that Buddha entered the city, I performed music and offered a single pellet of incense as an act of worship.

I dedicated this merit toward three goals: namely, to be forever free from all poverty and suffering, to constantly see the Buddhas and spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), and to always hear the True Dharma; it is for these reasons that I have obtained this retribution."
The commentary states:
"Passing through kalpas as numerous as the atoms of Buddha-fields" refers to being situated in delusion without yet having attained awakening; thus, they are called "dust-kalpas.
"There is a world named Perfectly Adorned" clarifies that the fundamental, universal radiance wisdom (*samantaprabhā-jñāna*) is itself the nature of reality, which is a world of boundless merit.

The Buddha named King of Universal Adornment of the Dharma-realm of Boundless Radiance is the stainless self-nature of the fundamental, universally luminous wisdom; it constantly illumines the dharma-realm and the realm of space, and all sentient beings share it equally. It is only because they dwell in delusion that they experience the differing karmic retributions of good and evil within the three realms and six paths.

If, for even a single thought-moment, one accords with the Chan of the innate self-nature—which is without cultivation or fabrication—then all mental states, objects, and sensory phenomena are by their very nature free from defilement, and one immediately realizes the Wisdom of Universal Radiance.

Its nature is inherently without dependence, relying neither on emptiness nor existence; yet it can universally illumine the dharma-realm of the ten directions with sovereign and wondrous function, naturally adorned with boundless merit.
It is simply that the fundamental essence is obscured by delusion, remaining inseparable from ignorance, greed, and hatred.

When a single thought of pure mind resolves this delusion and great wisdom manifests before one, one employs fifty dharma-gates—the ten abodes, ten practices, ten transferences, ten stages, and the stage of Equal Enlightenment—to harmonize wisdom and compassion according to their degree of maturity, thereby bringing about the conduct of Samantabhadra.

However, the essence of this wisdom does not depart from the initial mind; time does not shift, nor does the wisdom change. It merely causes the divine function of wisdom and compassion to gradually expand and gradually become more luminous, making it vast and penetrating, equal in measure to empty space and coextensive with the Dharma-realm. Sharing the minds of all sentient beings and abiding within all sentient beings, it manifests according to their minds, universally responding to the worlds of the ten directions, reaching everywhere without exception.
From beginning to end it is thus; its self-nature is eternally so, performing no transformations through the conceptualization of supernatural powers.
By the power of the roots of goodness of benevolence and compassion, it is naturally and perpetually so, until its meritorious practice is finally fulfilled.

This Elder Ratnaśikhin, through the dhyāna of the non-activity of the intrinsic nature of all sensory objects, has developed this wisdom of universal radiance to manifest and teach and transform all sentient beings.

Yet, when deluded, one speaks of kalpas as numerous as the atoms of a Buddha-field; once awakened, there is ultimately nothing of past or present. Advancement does not depart from this state: within the absence of past and present, there is a gradual unfolding, like clouds in the sky that gather and disperse without ever departing from the nature of space itself, yet the nature of space is not subject to temporal constraints.

Regarding the Buddha named King of the Universal Adornment of the Boundless Radiance Dharma-realm: when he entered the city, I performed music and burned a single pellet of incense as an offering to him. As for the merit obtained thereby, it serves merely to indicate that while musical sounds are objects of the five sensory realms, one thereby realizes that the fundamental nature of these five sensory objects is itself the Dharma-body.
This is originally the realm of the universal radiance-wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*; taking this as the joy of the Dharma is called "offering.

Those who attain this path dedicate [their merit] to three places: they forever leave behind poverty and suffering, constantly behold all Buddhas and spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and their boundless merits, and by means of this, they transform delusion into wisdom, thereby attaining the capacity to teach and transform sentient beings.
"I only know this liberation door of the treasury of immeasurable merit" and below, it clarifies the advancement through the recommendation of one's virtues.

By transforming the delusion of ignorance into understanding, one accomplishes the wisdom of universal radiance; employing this to teach and transform sentient beings constitutes the treasury of immeasurable merit.
The meditative body of the Elder Vimukticandra of the Ten Abodes contains oceans of ten Buddha-fields; taking the objective realm as following from the essence, it constitutes the meditative body.

Within these Ten Practices, the Elder Ratnaśikhin takes the meditative body as its functional application to constitute the meditative body, such that no sensory object of form is not subsumed within meditation.
The sixth is the practice of excellence (*sādhumatī*), which takes the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) as its primary element, with the other nine perfections as its companions.
The meaning of "South" is as explained previously.

There is a land named "Root of the Creeper" (*śālamūla*); this signifies that the wisdom of this stage is profound and firm, reaching down to the very limits of the waters and being impossible to uproot or overturn; thus it is called "Root of the Creeper."

As for the city named Pumen (Universal Gate), it is because this elder has nothing he does not master in the world and nothing he does not rescue; his medical arts for treating illness leave no disease unclarified; regarding the roots and dispositions of the Great, Small, and Single Vehicles, there are none to whom he does not show the way, guiding them according to the Dharma as appropriate to the time; and there is no fragrant water for bathing, famous fine garments, or food of the finest flavor that he does not provide as alms. Therefore, the city is named Pumen.

The elder named Universal Eye (Puyan) is so named because the wisdom of this stage is profound and subtle; there is nothing in the world he does not understand, and he clearly perceives all worldly phenomena throughout the ten directions—therefore, he is called Universal Eye.

In this stage, one brings to perfection all medical arts and all Buddhist teachings—both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna dharma-gates—as well as food, drink, and clothing, constantly bestowing them throughout the ten directions.
It also blends all fragrances to make offerings to the Buddhas.
This is explained extensively in the sutra texts.
From the passage "I only know this Dharma-door for causing all sentient beings to universally see all Buddhas with joy" onwards, it constitutes the advancement through the recommendation of virtues.

In this stage, after the practitioner has seen the Path, they bring all matters concerning the benefit of sentient beings to immediate clarity through their compassion, thereby benefiting all classes of beings.
In the tenth stage, the bhikṣu Ocean Banner enters the supernormal power of quiescent extinction and transforms and benefits beings throughout the ten directions.
At this stage, the elder Universal Eye universally delivers and saves all through the various vehicles of the Great and Small Right Dharma, as well as the various merits of worldly dharmas.
The seventh is the practice of non-attachment, for which the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*) is primary and the other nine are its companions.
The meaning of "South" is as explained previously.
There is a great city named Tālaketu, which in this language is translated as "Luminous Purity."
The king was named Analaṃkṛta (Unwearied).
In this stage, it is clarified that he governed the state's administration skillfully; out of compassion for all living beings, he never grew weary.
Because the world was filled with many acts of rebellion and many unwholesome deeds, he manifested a majestic and awe-inspiring presence.

He transformed his own body into a hundred thousand fierce soldiers, whose appearances were hideous and whose clothing was coarse and shabby; they brandished weapons, bared their arms, and glared with fury, wielding various instruments of torture that struck terror into all who saw them.

He transforms his own body to manifest various kinds of evil deeds, and then uses that very transformed body to pursue and seize them; he may cut off their ears and noses, gouge out their eyes, or subject them to various forms of painful treatment, so as to cause real sentient beings to fear and refrain from transgression, to grow weary of such acts and depart from them, and to be able to give rise to the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment.

This clarifies the practice of the Bodhisattva’s great kindness and great compassion used to subdue evil dharmas: manifesting awe-inspiring majesty outwardly while harboring compassion inwardly, he truly does not harm even a single flea or ant through his heart of great kindness and compassion, let alone a human being.
The details are as explained in the sutras.
From the passage "I have only attained this liberation door of illusion" onwards, this is the advancement through the attribution of virtues.

The eighth stage, the practice that is difficult to attain, takes the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*) as its primary element, with the other nine perfections serving as its companions.
The meaning of "namo" is as explained previously.
There is a city named Wondrous Light (Miaoguang), and its king is named Great Light (Daguang).
This Wondrous Light is the fundamental basis for formless shapes.
The King of Sublime Wisdom and Great Radiance (*Sudarśana-mahāprabha-rāja*) is the sovereign function of sublime wisdom; it is the wisdom of differentiation (*vibhakti-jñāna*).

By means of this stage, one accomplishes a portion of sublime practice that accords with principle and is effortless, yet there remains a predominance of the mind directed toward liberation. This differs from the eighth stage of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), where the effortless wisdom that accords with the Dharma manifests spontaneously. Fearing that one might become stagnant in great compassion by following the non-active nature of the essence of wisdom itself, [the practitioner] relies on the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*) from the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*) up through the ten stages to guard against such stagnation. Thus, upon reaching this stage, one recollects the power of original vows and initiates the practice of great compassion, ensuring that one does not dwell in mere purity.

In wisdom, compassion, and conduct, one gradually becomes increasingly sublime; yet on the path of great samādhi and nirvāṇa, the afflictions and habitual tendencies are not abandoned until the tenth bhūmi is fully perfected, at which point one attains mastery in the practices of Samantabhadra.
For one whose stage has not yet been perfected, the practices that assist the Path must not be neglected or abandoned.
For one who has already reached that stage, the practices that assist the Path must not be retained.
This is true for all worldly phenomena; it can be seen by reflecting upon them.

From the eighth stage of the ten abodes, the eighth of the ten practices, the eighth of the ten dedications, and the eighth of the ten grounds, each according to its respective position, there is a portion of effortless wisdom that harmonizes with the practice of compassionate wisdom.

The essence of superiority and inferiority is as follows: in the seventh stage of the Ten Abodes, the laywoman Śreṣṭhadattā dwells together with the seer of the eighth stage at the place of the ocean tide, because wisdom and compassion are non-dual in essence.

Regarding the seventh and eighth stages of these ten stages of practice, the King of Insatiable Radiance in the City of Pure Illumination and the Great Radiance King are brought together to manifest the essence of great compassion; they employ the hermit and the king respectively to represent the superior and inferior qualities of each stage.
The functions and powers of the practices differ according to their respective stages; all stages should be understood in this manner.
The Path has no dual essence; it merely clarifies the distinct excellence of each stage.

As seen in the seventh and eighth [chapters] of the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, where the Bodhisattvas Avalokiteśvara and Samantagāmin appear together in an assembly, they are represented by noble beings (*ārya*).
This is because one gradually enters the divine state, as that which is employed therein is profound, subtle, and vast.
Regarding the city of Wondrous Light being ten yojanas in length and breadth: both "one" and "ten" are the mothers of all great numbers.
A "mother" signifies the source; it is fundamental wisdom.

The ten billion pathways represent the myriad practices within the wisdom of differentiation; they clarify that while these practices do not depart from the essence of the fundamental wondrous wisdom, they manifest as the vast function of boundless practices.
This is because the first [number] and the tenth represent the general principle of all numbers, from ten billion and ten unspeakable [numbers] up to the entirety of all numerical magnitudes.

Regarding the statement that between each and every path there are immeasurable billions of sentient beings: this clarifies that within the wisdom of discernment and among the various practices, each individual practice gathers and transforms immeasurable billions of sentient beings, so that those with differing faculties and desires may all find their proper place.

The various adornments of the assembly described below are all obtained as the retributive fruit of the practices of wisdom and compassion, as detailed in the sutra; one may know the cause by observing the result.

As for the King’s twenty-eight marks, they clarify that the two types of practice—the practice of future wholesome dharmas and the practice of reality—are not yet perfected. Since there are causes and fruits within each of these practices, it is because he lacks these four sets of cause and effect that he does not possess the thirty-two marks.

This clarifies that the fulfillment of the latter two kinds of practice means that transformative activity has become all-pervasive and the thirty-two marks are also perfected, because one does not abide within the pavilion of great wisdom.

Because he has universally practiced the conduct encompassed by the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) and the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) at the crossroads of the world, he is endowed with all the marks of perfection.

Within this City of Sublime Light, there is a pavilion named Treasury of the True Dharma, adorned with incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) jewels; its radiance is brilliant and peerless, such that sentient beings who behold it can never tire of it.
Regarding the Great Radiance King situated in the center: the pavilions represent fundamental universal radiance wisdom, while the Great Radiance King represents differentiated wisdom.
Within the city are countless jewel pavilions, all of which are born as the retributive fruits of the ten *pāramitā* practices in their respective original positions.
Dwelling at the very center of the city within the pavilions is the retributive body (*vipākakāya*) of fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*).

As for the Great Radiance King, who sits upon a lion throne of wish-fulfilling *maṇi* jewel lotuses not far from his dwelling pavilion: he is said to be "not far" because of his non-abiding wisdom (*apratiṣṭhita-jñāna*), which is pure; he uses the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) to gather and transform sentient beings as the four crossroads; and he is called a "wish-fulfilling jewel" because he benefits sentient beings according to their wishes.
Wisdom is eternally stainless and is called the *maṇi* jewel.
Constantly dwelling in the world yet remaining undefiled, it is the vast lotus throne.
Each city appears according to the karmic power of sentient beings, differing in purity and impurity.

Regarding "entering the samādhi that accords with the world, headed by great compassion": this clarifies that one does not abide in pure wisdom but practices compassion in accordance with the conventional world to benefit sentient beings; because the mind is free from sinking or agitation, it is called samādhi. This is termed the Bodhisattva’s banner-like practice of the samādhi that accords with the world.

When he entered this samādhi, the city, both inside and out, shook in six ways; the trees, pavilions, and all surrounding realms leaned their bodies toward the king and prostrated themselves before him.
This is brought about by the power of this samādhi; its details are found extensively in the sūtra text.
From the passage "I only know this gate of the samādhi that takes great compassion as its foremost and accords with the world" onwards, it concerns the recommendation of virtues and advancement.
In this stage, one clearly abides in pure wisdom that does not dwell [in extremes], as the practice of compassion and mercy pervades all in accordance with worldly convention.
In the ninth stage, the Practice of Goodness (*sādhumatī*), the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*) is primary, while the other nine serve as its companions.
The meaning of "South" (Nan) is as explained previously.

There is a royal capital named Anzhu (Abiding Securely); among the five ranks, this is exclusively the ninth, which is the rank of the Dharma King. Because one who has attained clarity and reaches this stage possesses mastery in preaching the Dharma, it is designated as a "royal capital."
His conduct as abbot was characterized by the tranquility of body and mind; thus he was named Anzhu (Peacefully Abiding), which illustrates the master’s resolute virtue.
There was a laywoman named Budong (Immovable), who illustrated the master’s compassionate, harmonious, joyful, and gentle character.
The mind does not follow external objects; this illustrates the conduct of a Dharma Master.
This is exemplified by the laywoman Acalā, yet it does not necessarily require a woman to be a Dharma Master.
The upāsikā said, "I do not give rise to anger or resentment even toward my own kinsmen, much less toward other sentient beings.

Sudhana marveled at this woman’s threefold practice and spoke in verse: "Guarding the pure precepts, Cultivating vast patience, And practicing diligence without regression— Her radiance illuminates the world."

As for Sudhana’s seeing the upāsikā and merely joining his palms in reverence without performing a prostration: this is because the teaching is expounded from the perspective of this stage, which possesses no nature of high or low; thus he does not perform the formal ritual of bowing, just as one who has attained the equality of essence and characteristics—free from self and person—as described in the *Caryāgītikoṣa* (The Song of Conduct).
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Tathāgata as he is perceived should not be paid homage.
For this reason, it is titled the *Acarita-sūtra* (The Sutra on Non-action).
This ultimate Way is the unsurpassed rite.
It requires merely joining the palms and contemplating how one accords with the Way, for its essence is equanimous.
Wisdom and compassion do not require the performance of formal, ritualized etiquette; it is only after attaining the Dharma that one follows worldly customs, departing with a formal bow.
The rank of a Dharma Master consists of ten types of practice: first, compassion; second, gentleness; third, humility and respect;

fourth, having a mind that remains unshaken amidst the realm of forms; fifth, upholding the precepts; sixth, patience; seventh, diligence; eighth, extensively elucidating the gates of remedial methods for all mundane and supramundane dharmas; ninth, skillfully expounding the four analytical knowledges with clarity; and tenth, possessing a voice that is harmonious and pleasant, bringing comfort and inquiry to others. These constitute the aspirations and virtues of a Dharma Master.

"From 'I have only attained this Samādhi-light of insatiable seeking for all dharmas' and 'having preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings so that they may all rejoice,' and following, is the section on advancing by extolling one's own virtues."
The scope of this Dharma Master’s position is vast and is fully contained within the scriptural text.

For now, we shall briefly understand the general meaning and sequence of the sutra; may all who compose [commentaries] rely well upon the original scripture to examine it with further precision and exhort their own resolve.
This upāsikā said:

"At that time, throughout the kalpa, she upheld the Dharma-gates taught by the Tathāgata without ever abandoning or discarding a single word or a single letter; this was likewise true even for mundane scripts, and even for the arts and crafts of the world—in each and every such discipline, it was likewise so."
By observing these ancient models, one should exert oneself in one's own person.
The tenth, the practice of reality, has the perfection of wisdom as its primary element, with the other nine as its companions.
The meaning of "Namo" is as explained previously.
There is a great city named Aparāntaka-dhāraṇī, which in this language means "Possessing Immeasurable Great Joy and Happiness.

Because one practices for the sake of such spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) by employing the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*)—namely, right action through shared purpose, kind speech, and skillful means—all sentient beings who see it receive benefit; therefore, the city is named "Possessing Joy and Happiness."

There is a renunciant non-Buddhist practitioner named Pūrvavilaṅghin; because he does not cling to the three realms, he is called a renunciant, and because his conduct is identical to that of all sentient beings, he is named Pūrvavilaṅghin ("One Who Transcends All").
Within the trichiliocosm, he practices in concert with all ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist outsiders; therefore, he is named Sarvagāmin (The All-Walker).
Upon the level ground at the summit of the mountain, he practices the *cankrama* (walking meditation) by means of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Wisdom that transcends the mundane is called the mountain peak.
Great Compassion that impartially gathers all sentient beings is called the level ground.

Through wisdom that is without dependence, the Good Spiritual Friend constantly manifests his body among all sentient beings—men and women, great and small—in the cities, towns, and villages of this Jambudvīpa, appearing in forms identical to their own species to preach the Dharma for them.
All sentient beings are entirely unable to know from where I have come; I merely cause those who hear me to practice according to reality.
Throughout all worlds in the ten directions, among humans, devas, and the six realms of existence, it is always thus; therefore, I am called "The Universal Walker" (Samantagāmin).
From the passage "From me, who only knows this" down to "the bodhisattva practice that reaches all places," this is the advancement through the cultivation of virtues.
The ten spiritual friends mentioned above have accomplished the worldly arts and practices of governance and transformation, while simultaneously cultivating a great deal of supramundane resolve.

If one constantly remains within the ocean of birth-and-death suffering, neither emerging nor sinking, thereby accomplishing the great wisdom, great compassion, and the ocean of all-knowledge, it is only in the subsequent stage that this is clearly realized.
